title: Case for Saying Less
author: Greg McKeown
summary: McKeown's 1-Minute Wednesday turns on a cognitive-science claim: when people look confused, our reflex is to explain more, yet research shows additional well-intentioned explanation often makes confusion worse. The mechanism is not intelligence or motivation but working-memory capacity; once working memory is flooded, the brain shifts from understanding to coping and additional words become noise crowding out the signal the listener is trying to hold. Clarity is produced not by effort but by restraint. The leader who says one clear thing and stops is easier to follow than one who says five adjacent things and hopes one lands. The diagnosis extends into everyday settings: long explanations blur rather than clarify, meetings drift even when everyone means well, good ideas lose their edge the moment they are over-defended. The practical prescription is brief: before explaining, pause and ask what the one idea is that actually matters right now, say that, then resist the urge to add more. Restraint is not an absence of effort; it is a form of attention directed at what the listener can actually hold.

quotes: When people don’t understand, explaining more usually makes it worse.
When someone looks confused, we assume the problem is a lack of explanation. That assumption is usually wrong. It’s a habit built over years of good intentions.

Controlled experiments in cognitive science point to a quieter truth. When researchers gave people additional explanations they believed would help, comprehension actually declined. Not slightly. Reliably.” “The issue wasn’t intelligence or motivation. It was capacity. Working memory is limited. When it’s flooded, the brain shifts from understanding to coping.
When unnecessary information is removed, understanding improves. People make better decisions because they can grasp the core more quickly.
This is why long explanations blur instead of clarify. It’s why meetings drift even when everyone means well, and why good ideas lose their edge the moment we over-defend them.
Clarity isn’t created by effort. It’s created by restraint.
You don’t need to say everything you know. You need to protect what matters most.” Archived from 1-Minute Wednesday (gregmckeown.com) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
